facts.text: The planning fallacy is the proven habit of underestimating the duration of one's own work; reference class forecasting corrects it using actual durations of similar past projects, while P50 and P80 dates indicate a 50% and 80% chance of finishing by those dates.
facts.quote: The planning fallacy is the proven human habit of underestimating how long one's own work will take; reference class forecasting corrects it by looking at how long similar past projects actually took; and P50 and P80 dates state the finish date with a 50% and an 80% chance of being met.

facts.text: In the 1994 experiments by Buehler, Griffin and Ross, only 29.7% of students finished their thesis by their own best-estimate date.
facts.quote: In the classic 1994 experiments by Buehler, Griffin and Ross, only 29.7% of students finished their thesis by their own "best estimate" date

facts.text: Students in the 1994 Buehler, Griffin and Ross experiments continued underestimating completion time even when told to be pessimistic and focused on their plan rather than past task outcomes. The booklet rates the planning-fallacy finding as proven.
facts.quote: they kept underestimating even when told to be pessimistic, and they focused on their plan rather than on how past tasks had gone. The booklet rates this as proven [Chapter 12].

facts.text: Kahneman and Lovallo called the remedy for the planning fallacy the outside view, which Flyvbjerg formalized as reference class forecasting: estimate from the actual outcome distribution of comparable past projects, then adjust, rather than estimating from internal plan details.
facts.quote: The remedy Kahneman and Lovallo called the outside view, and Flyvbjerg formalized as reference class forecasting: do not estimate from the inside details of your plan, estimate from the actual distribution of outcomes of comparable past projects, then adjust.

facts.text: The United Kingdom Treasury applies reference-class-based uplifts to public projects.
facts.quote: The United Kingdom Treasury applies such uplifts to public projects.

facts.text: Reference class forecasting outperformed Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting in accuracy only when the reference class was genuinely similar; a 2025 review concluded that reference class forecasting works only if the right reference classes have been constructed.
facts.quote: reference class forecasting beat Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting on accuracy only when the reference class was genuinely similar, and a 2025 review concludes it works "only if the right reference classes have been constructed"

facts.text: The behavioral explanation for reference class forecasting is contested.
Chapter 13 found no reference class of first-time virtual-validation programs meeting a four-month window and calls the four months a target, not a forecast.
facts.quote: no reference class of first-time virtual-validation programs meeting a four-month window exists; Chapter 13 states that none was found and calls the four months "a target, not a forecast".

facts.text: The booklet recommends decomposing virtual-validation schedule estimates into components with historical evidence: machine-model development, supplier sensor-model deliveries, rig commissioning, software and hardware procurement, hazard-analysis campaigns, correlation projects, data pipelines, assessor reviews, test automation and hiring. An uplift should be openly stated where data are thin.
facts.quote: rig commissioning, software and hardware procurement lead times, hazard-analysis campaigns, earlier correlation projects, data-pipeline work, past assessor review durations, test automation, and hiring lead times, with an openly stated uplift where data are thin [Chapter 12].

facts.text: The gap between a program's P50 and P80 completion dates measures schedule uncertainty.
facts.quote: The gap between them is a measure of uncertainty.

facts.text: A credible schedule statement should give a median readiness date, an 80%-confidence date and the probability of meeting the gate, rather than a single date. These values must come from the program's own schedule model.
facts.quote: "a median readiness date of March X, an 80%-confidence date of April Y, and a Z% probability of meeting the April gate." The values must come from the program's own schedule model.

facts.text: Experiments found that numeric schedule ranges preserved trust better than verbal hedges.
facts.quote: Numeric ranges like these preserved trust better than verbal hedges in experiments

facts.text: Estimators' own nominal 90% confidence ranges are known to be far too narrow.
facts.quote: estimators' own "90%" confidence ranges are known to be far too narrow [Chapter 12].

facts.text: The booklet asks the executive brief to show P50 and P80 dates for both the end of preparation and the end of delivery, descoping steps that keep P80 inside the deadline, and the current probability of meeting the fixed date rather than the planned date.
facts.quote: show P50 and P80 dates for the end of preparation and the end of delivery, the descoping steps that keep the P80 date inside the deadline, and the current probability of making the fixed date rather than the planned one [Chapter 12].
